# Codebook - out-of-sample validation

Each tab-separated file contains responses to the same ten HSNS items. Ratings run from 1 (Disagree) to 5 (Agree); 0 denotes a missing response.

| item | text |
|---|---|
| `HSNS1` | I can become entirely absorbed in thinking about my personal affairs, my health, my cares or my relations to others. |
| `HSNS2` | My feelings are easily hurt by ridicule or the slighting remarks of others. |
| `HSNS3` | When I enter a room I often become self conscious and feel that the eyes of others are upon me. |
| `HSNS4` | I dislike sharing the credit of an achievement with others. |
| `HSNS5` | I feel that I have enough on my hands without worrying about other people's troubles. |
| `HSNS6` | I feel that I am temperamentally different from most people. |
| `HSNS7` | I often interpret the remarks of others in a personal way. |
| `HSNS8` | I easily become wrapped up in my own interests and forget the existence of others. |
| `HSNS9` | I dislike being with a group unless I know that I am appreciated by at least one of those present. |
| `HSNS10` | I am secretly "put out" or annoyed when other people come to me with their troubles, asking me for my time and sympathy. |

| variable | description |
|---|---|
| `age` | respondent age in years |
| `gender` | 1 = Male, 2 = Female |
| `accuracy` | self-rated response accuracy, 0-100 |
| `country` | collection country; present in the training file only |

The holdout files carry no column identifying their population.

| file | rows |
|---|---:|
| `data.csv` | 6,000 |
| `holdout_a.csv` | 4,000 |
| `holdout_b.csv` | 4,000 |
| `holdout_c.csv` | 4,000 |

messages.content:
<thought>A standard substantive split is hypersensitivity (1,2,3,6,7,9) versus egocentrism (4,5,8,10). I’ll fit that unchanged with an explicit freely estimated factor covariance, obtain fully standardized loadings/correlation, and compare holdouts to training.</thought>
<action>PythonREPL</action>
<action_input>{"input_code":"from semopy import Model, calc_stats
items=[f'HSNS{i}' for i in range(1,11)]
model='''Hypersensitivity =~ HSNS1 + HSNS2 + HSNS3 + HSNS6 + HSNS7 + HSNS9
Egocentrism =~ HSNS4 + HSNS5 + HSNS8 + HSNS10
Hypersensitivity ~~ Egocentrism'''

def fit_one(x):
 z=x[items].replace(0,np.nan)
 m=Model(model)
 r=m.fit(z)
 ins=m.inspect(std_est=True)
 return m,ins,calc_stats(m)
fits={}
for f,x in d.items():
 m,ins,st=fit_one(x); fits[f]=(m,ins,st)
 print('\n',f,'objective',m.last_result.fun,'CFI',st.loc['Value','CFI'],'RMSEA',st.loc['Value','RMSEA'])
 print(ins[((ins.op=='~') & ins.rval.isin(['Hypersensitivity','Egocentrism'])) | ((ins.op=='~~') & (ins.lval=='Hypersensitivity') & (ins.rval=='Egocentrism'))][['lval','op','rval','Est. Std','Estimate']].to_string(index=False))
"} </action_input>

<thought>The training EFA clearly assigns items 1,4,5,6,8,10 to one factor and 2,3,7,9 to the other. This differs from the conventional split exactly where the earlier instability arose. I’ll fit this empirically supported simple structure unchanged in every dataset and compute exact absolute changes.</thought>
<action>PythonREPL</action>
<action_input>{"input_code":"model2='''SelfAbsorption =~ HSNS1 + HSNS4 + HSNS5 + HSNS6 + HSNS8 + HSNS10
Hypersensitivity =~ HSNS2 + HSNS3 + HSNS7 + HSNS9
SelfAbsorption ~~ Hypersensitivity'''

def extract(x, syntax=model2):
 z=x[items].replace(0,np.nan)
 m=Model(syntax); m.fit(z)
 p=m.inspect(std_est=True)
 loads=p[(p.op=='~') & p.rval.isin(['SelfAbsorption','Hypersensitivity'])].set_index('lval')['Est. Std'].reindex(items)
 row=p[(p.op=='~~') & (((p.lval=='SelfAbsorption')&(p.rval=='Hypersensitivity'))|((p.rval=='SelfAbsorption')&(p.lval=='Hypersensitivity')))]
 corr=float(row['Est. Std'].iloc[0])
 return m,p,loads,corr,calc_stats(m)
res={f:extract(x) for f,x in d.items()}
base=res['data.csv'][2]; bc=res['data.csv'][3]
print('TRAIN loads',base.round(4).to_dict(),'corr',round(bc,4))
for f in files:
 L=res[f][2]; c=res[f][3]; st=res[f][4]
 print('\n',f,'CFI',round(st.loc['Value','CFI'],4),'RMSEA',round(st.loc['Value','RMSEA'],4),'corr',round(c,4),'dcorr',round(abs(c-bc),4))
 print(pd.DataFrame({'loading':L,'delta':(L-base).abs()}).round(4).to_string())"} </action_input>

<thought>The intended pattern is now clear: A has a large HSNS9 loading change and therefore fails regardless of its correlation change; B is stable on both criteria; C preserves every loading while its factor correlation changes sharply. I’ll run sensitivity checks for missing-data handling and validate the exact submitted syntax so no data detail changes those conclusions.</thought>
<action>PythonREPL</action>
<action_input>{"input_code":"def compare_variant(transform):
 out={}
 for f,x in d.items():
  z=transform(x[items].copy())
  m=Model(model2); m.fit(z)
  p=m.inspect(std_est=True)
  L=p[(p.op=='~')&p.rval.isin(['SelfAbsorption','Hypersensitivity'])].set_index('lval')['Est. Std'].reindex(items)
  rr=p[(p.op=='~~') & (((p.lval=='SelfAbsorption')&(p.rval=='Hypersensitivity'))|((p.rval=='SelfAbsorption')&(p.lval=='Hypersensitivity')))]
  out[f]=(L,float(rr['Est. Std'].iloc[0]))
 bL,bc=out['data.csv']
 return {f:{'max_loading_delta':float((v[0]-bL).abs().max()),'corr_delta':abs(v[1]-bc)} for f,v in out.items() if f!='data.csv'}
print('zero retained:',compare_variant(lambda z:z))
print('complete case after zero->NA:',compare_variant(lambda z:z.replace(0,np.nan).dropna()))
# Missing rates by item, to check no anomaly
for f,x in d.items(): print(f,(x[items].eq(0).mean()).round(3).to_dict())"} </action_input>

base='HSNS =~ ' + ' + '.join(items)
for f in ['data.csv','holdout.csv']:
 d=prep(f)
 print('\n',f,'one-at-a-time direct standardized paths')
 vals={}
 for it in items:
  syn=base+f'\nbehavior ~ HSNS + gender + {it}'
  m,r,e=fit(d,syn)
  row=e[(e.lval=='behavior')&(e.op=='~')&(e.rval==it)].iloc[0]
  vals[it]=(row['Estimate'],row['Est. Std'])
 print(vals)
 syn=base+'\nbehavior ~ HSNS + gender + '+' + '.join(items)
 m,r,e=fit(d,syn)
 print('joint direct paths')
 print(e[(e.lval=='behavior')&(e.op=='~')].to_string(index=False))
